criteria.name: Introduction: mission concept and rationale. Include the following required information: What is the spacecraft's primary mission? Why is the mission needed? How many spacecraft are used and why? Who are the users (operator and customers)?
criteria.reasoning: All four required items (primary mission, rationale, spacecraft number, users) are addressed in detail with specific facts and literature references [1]-[6]. Rationale links bleaching detection gap to mission need. Only minor further depth on user needs analysis would raise it to 10.

evidence.quote: The primary mission of ZYZZsat is to image the whole Great Barrier Reef in visible bands at 5 m resolution
The operator is the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS)... The customers are the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority
One satellite is therefore used. This also simplifies communications, reduces cost

criteria.name: Main body: mission design. Present a summary of the mission design using software and/or hand calculations as appropriate. Include relevant screenshots and software files in the main body of the report and/or appendix. Include the following information: Where will it launch from, and using which launch vehicle? Why did you choose this option? What type of orbit will you use? What are its characteristics and orbital elements? Will you need to perform any orbital maneuvers? Which ground control facilities will you use? How often will your spacecraft be able to communicate with ground control? How long will the mission last, and what are your plans for EOL?
criteria.reasoning: All major requirements addressed: launch site/vehicle with justified trade (Table 2), orbit type, elements (Table 4), hand-verified J2 sun-synchronous inclination, no-manoeuvre justification, STK access analysis, data budget, 5-year duration and drag-sail EOL. STK screenshots and appendix files provided. Hand calculations (decay, swath, azimuth) check out. Link budget explicitly deferred, a minor gap.

evidence.quote: The baseline is an SSMS rideshare flight on Vega C from Kourou in early 2025
There are six passes each day, three in the evening and three in the morning (UTC), and the mean pass lasts 580.8 s
With a 4 m² sail the satellite re-enters about two years after the end of the mission.

criteria.name: Conclusion
criteria.reasoning: Conclusions are specific and quantitative, drawn directly from the report's evidence, and honestly identify four limitations with mitigation paths (fallback launcher, unproven fluid lensing, missing link budget, coverage rate). Not generic.

evidence.quote: A 600 km sun-synchronous orbit at 97.79° inclination gives the same morning lighting on every pass
The design has four limitations. First, Vega C has not yet flown

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: Clear structure with executive summary, numbered sections, consistently labelled and referenced figures/tables, IEEE-style citations [1]-[15] all matching in-text usage. Writing is precise and professional. Some references are loosely specified (e.g. 'Nature, news article', 'The Space Review, article 3887'), preventing a 10.

evidence.quote: This report presents the design of ZYZZsat... a single Earth observation microsatellite for monitoring coral bleaching
Figure 2: Inclination required for a sun-synchronous orbit as a function of altitude.
[11] D. A. Vallado, Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications, 4th ed.

requirements.where: Images 1-5; Appendix A lists STK files in ZYZZsat_STK.zip

technical_issues.issue: Link budget for the X-band downlink is not calculated (acknowledged by the student); the 50 Mbit/s rate and 3.5x margin are asserted without link closure.
Decay calculation uses a single mean density and constant scale height; solar-cycle variability acknowledged but lifetime figures are order-of-magnitude only.
Access statistics derived from only two days of STK data; pass frequency claim generalised from a short sample.
Vega C flight record stated as of 2020; baseline relies on a vehicle not yet flown at time of writing (fallback provided, so acceptable).

overall: An excellent, comprehensive mission design report. All task requirements are met with verified hand calculations, STK evidence, honest limitations, and professional presentation. Minor gaps (link budget, short access sample, some vague references) keep it just below full marks.

feedback.summary: Excellent work on the ZYZZsat mission design report. All required elements are addressed with strong justification, verified hand calculations, and clear STK evidence. Your honest treatment of limitations is a real strength. To reach the top band, close the remaining analytical gaps: complete the X-band link budget, extend the access analysis beyond two days, and tighten reference details.
next_steps: Complete the X-band downlink link budget in Section 2.4 so the 50 Mbit/s rate and 3.5x margin are demonstrated by link closure rather than asserted.
Extend the STK access analysis beyond the two-day sample (e.g. a full repeat cycle or season) before generalising the six-passes-per-day claim in Table 5.
Refine loosely specified bibliography entries (e.g. 'Nature, news article', 'The Space Review, article 3887') with full author, title, date and URL/DOI details.

criteria.C1: Your introduction addresses all four requirements in detail: the 5 m GBR imaging mission, the bleaching-detection rationale, the single-satellite choice with cost/communications justification, and clearly named operator (AIMS) and customers. Literature references [1]-[6] support the discussion well. For full marks, deepen the user needs analysis - e.g. quantify how the 5 m resolution and revisit meet AIMS and GBRMPA monitoring requirements.
criteria.C2: A comprehensive, well-evidenced design: justified Vega C/Kourou trade (Table 2), orbit elements (Table 4), hand-verified sun-synchronous inclination, a clear no-manoeuvre argument, STK access statistics, data budget, and drag-sail EOL. Screenshots and appendix STK files support the work. The uncalculated X-band link budget and the two-day access sample are the main gaps preventing full marks; also note the Vega C flight-record caveat is handled acceptably via your fallback.
criteria.C3: Your conclusions are specific and quantitative, tracing directly to the evidence (e.g. the 600 km, 97.79 degree orbit giving consistent morning lighting), and you honestly identify four limitations with mitigation paths. This is well above generic. To reach full marks, tie each limitation to a concrete next action or design iteration step, showing how the design would be refined.
criteria.C4: The report is professionally structured with an executive summary, numbered sections, consistently labelled figures and tables, and IEEE-style citations [1]-[15] that match in-text usage. Writing is precise throughout. The barrier to full marks is reference completeness: several entries are loosely specified, so tighten them to full bibliographic standard. Otherwise, formatting and presentation are exemplary.
